title: One, two, five
hookLine: Bhai Gurdas says one Sikh is a Sikh, two are a sangat, and where five gather the Lord is present (Bhai Gurdas, Var 13)

cards: One chair by a window, someone reading alone. A second chair pulled up, and now there's a conversation. Three more, and suddenly it's a gathering, and the room feels different.

Nothing about the furniture changed. Bhai Gurdas noticed what changes when people add up, and he put it in a line short enough to say in a single breath, a line that simply counts, the way a child counts on her fingers.

teach.b: It's in his thirteenth var. Bhai Gurdas says: one is a Sikh.
Two are a sadh sangat, a holy company.

teach.h: WHERE FIVE ARE, THERE IS GOD.
teach.b: And where five are, there is God. Take the steps one at a time. One is a Sikh.
A single person, alone, early in the morning, remembering, is already a Sikh. Nobody needs a crowd to be on the path. Two are a sangat.
The moment a second person joins, it's no longer just practice. It's company.

Two people reading a line of the Guru's word together, or singing it softly in a kitchen, already make the thing Bhai Gurdas praises in his vars. And then, five. Where five gather, he says, God is present.
Not that God is absent from the one, or the two. The line climbs, the way a person climbs stairs, and at the top is the plainest promise of the three.
Some readers hear in it an old Punjabi way of speaking about a village council of five, where God was said to sit among the five.
Some also hear it ahead of a moment later in the Sikh story, when five Sikhs stand together at the heart of the Khalsa. Bhai Gurdas doesn't spell out either one. His line simply counts.
What's striking is how small his numbers are. He doesn't say a thousand, or a full gurdwara, or a festival crowd.
He says five: a gathering that fits around one table. In Bhai Gurdas's arithmetic, the holy company was never about size. It starts with one, becomes real with two, and five is enough.

how: Sikhs gather in sangats of every size, from a family reading together at home to a full gurdwara, and Bhai Gurdas's line is quoted for the worth of even a small gathering.

o: the One God, who is present only where five meet
the first of five Sikh rules for a gathering
the first step: one is a Sikh, two a holy company

games.q: Bhai Gurdas's count — tap the pairs.

s: Bhai Gurdas says it takes a big crowd to make a sangat
two are a sadh sangat, in his count.
in Bhai Gurdas's line, one person alone is already a Sikh
the count starts there: one is a Sikh.
Bhai Gurdas says God is present where five gather
that's the top step of the count in his thirteenth var.

games.q: you want to gather people around the Guru's word. how many do you wait for?
o: a full hall, or it isn't worth it.
one other person: two are a sangat.
no one: it only counts alone.
games.why: in Bhai Gurdas's count, one is a Sikh, two are a sangat, and where five are, there is God. the numbers are small on purpose.

practice: Picture two people you could sit with this week, at a table, on a call, on a bench, for something small and shared: a meal, a walk, a song, a reading, a few minutes of quiet together.
See their faces, and notice how the room changes when you picture three chairs instead of one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for the three of you.

wordCard.voice: One. The first step in Bhai Gurdas's count: one is a Sikh, two are a holy company, and where five are, there is God.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: five. The top of Bhai Gurdas's count.

carryVoice: Your line: where five gather. Small numbers, chosen on purpose, around one table. Day seven hundred ten, done.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 13, pauri 19 (one a Sikh, two a sadh sangat, in five God)
